transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-04-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: 58 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Torres (CTO - CascadeAI), Mark Li (Head of ML), Sana Ahmed (Platform Eng), Tom Becker (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — confirm success criteria for the POC, get the workload sizing and burst profile, and align on capacity/autoscale options and timelines. Ravi's going to walk through the perf plan.

[00:15] Elena Torres: Thanks Maya. Quick context: CascadeAI is building a customer-facing RAG assistant for support. We're replacing a partly in-house infra now. Primary concerns are p95 latency under load, cost, and data residency/compliance. We want the POC to be realistic — production‑like traffic for two weeks.

[00:40] Maya Chen: Perfect, and what's your expected load? average qps, peak?

[00:47] Mark Li: So baseline is about 30 QPS avg during business hours, peak spikes up to ~200 QPS during events, but those are short — like 5–10 minutes. Token length average is ~120 tokens per response, occasional long ones to 800 tokens.

[01:10] Ravi Patel: Good — that's helpful. For sizing we typically look at steady-state concurrency and peak burst. Two axes we'll consider: reserved GPU capacity (to cover steady and near‑steady load) and burst capacity to handle spikes. For model, which checkpoint are you planning to serve?

[01:25] Mark Li: We're testing an open Llama-style 70B variant fine-tuned for RAG. Latency target is p95 < 250ms for short responses (~120 tokens) and p95 < 700ms for long responses (up to 800 tokens).

[01:45] Ravi Patel: Ok — 70B will need H100/A100 class. For 120-token responses, with batching and KV-cache warm, a single A100-80GB host can do roughly X concurrent small requests depending on quantization. If you quantize to int8 or 4-bit, throughput improves but we need to validate quality.

[02:08] Tom Becker: Can you clarify the quantization tradeoff? We can't degrade accuracy beyond ~1% of our baseline.

[02:15] Ravi Patel: Sure. In our experience: 8-bit dynamic quant gives decent token throughput with minimal quality loss; 4-bit techniques (GPTQ-style) give big performance gains but risk edge-case regressions. SE-led bench will run exact evals against your pass/fail prompts. We'll capture quality metrics (EM, BLEU-ish or your custom ranking metric) alongside latency.

[02:40] Elena Torres: On capacity models — what's your recommended reserved vs burst split for a customer with our profile?

[02:48] Maya Chen: We usually recommend sizing reserved GPUs to cover about 70–80% of expected sustained load during business hours and then enable burst capacity for short peaks. Reserved ensures predictable latency and cost; burst gives headroom without big commit.

[03:05] Ravi Patel: Practically, for your numbers — if avg 30 QPS and peaks to 200 for short periods — we might reserve capacity equivalent to ~6 A100 instances to get steady throughput with KV caching and batching tuned, and allow burst to scale up to 20–24 instances during events. We'll validate exact numbers in benchmarks.

[03:30] Sana Ahmed: Are these GPU counts per model replica or per shard? We have some constraints on VPC egress and inter-node network.

[03:38] Ravi Patel: Good question. That estimate assumes single-replica serving with model sharding where necessary; if you use tensor-parallel shards the cfg changes. We'll map to your infra in the bench (H100 vs A100, number of GPUs per host). On VPC — Redwood Private supports VPC peering or customer's VPC control plane; we can run the POC on Redwood Dedicated if you want reserved capacity in a customer-isolated pool.

[04:05] Mark Li: What about autoscale ramp times? Cold-starts on large models scare me — I've seen seconds-to-minutes.

[04:12] Ravi Patel: Warm pools are key. Our autoscaler keeps a small warm pool of standby model instances (configurable) to serve sudden spikes within low latency — think fast scale-up in ~15–45s depending on model size and whether KV caches need to be warmed. For very short spikes (under 10s) we recommend burst routing to a hosted compact model variant for graceful degradation.

[04:40] Tom Becker: So fallback strategy could be: reserved full model -> warm pool to scale -> if still overloaded route to smaller quantized variant or fallback to a hosted cheaper LLM?

[04:50] Ravi Patel: Exactly. Typical policy: targets p95 SLO by preferring warm pool and autoscale; if remaining capacity is insufficient and latency would exceed threshold, automatically route to compatible model variant (lower-precision or smaller architecture), or to a hosted Redwood fallback model. This keeps the application online while we avoid catastrophic latency spikes.

[05:15] Elena Torres: How do you measure and expose those metrics? We need token-level cost, per-route latency, and per-model error rates.

[05:22] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, and can annotate regressions against a held-out prompt set. We'll attach that to the POC so you can see end-to-end.

[05:35] Sana Ahmed: Security — do you support KMS integration and audit logs for the POC? We require SOC 2 evidence, SSO, and audit trails to sign off.

[05:44] Maya Chen: Yes. For Dedicated/Private POC we'd enable KMS integration, SAML SSO, RBAC, and provide audit logs. I'll add the security pack link after the call. For hosted POC we can do encryption in transit and at rest and customer-managed keys with our Private offering.

[06:05] Mark Li: For the benchmark itself, what tests will you run? We want throughput, p95/p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens, and quality regression checks.

[06:15] Ravi Patel: We'll run a matrix: baseline (no quantization) vs int8 dynamic vs 4-bit GPTQ; batch sizes [1,4,8,16]; steady-state load at average QPS, sustained high QPS, and burst spikes. We'll collect p50/95/99 latencies, tail behaviors, GPU utilization, and tokens/sec. We'll also run your representative prompt set through each config to compute quality deltas.

[06:45] Elena Torres: How long does the POC need to run to be meaningful? Two weeks was our ask.

[06:52] Maya Chen: Two weeks is fine — we typically do a week of perf runs plus one week of validation and production-like testing. If you want continuous traffic patterns over weekends we can simulate that as well.

[07:05] Tom Becker: Cost — can you give us a rough model for reserved vs burst? Even a ballpark helps to make an internal case.

[07:12] Maya Chen: We'll put numbers in the POC pricing doc, but ballpark: reserved capacity comes with a monthly commit and lower per-token cost. Burst is metered at on-demand rates. For decisioning, we'll show expected monthly cost under your traffic profile for both 70% reserved and 100% reserved scenarios.

[07:35] Mark Li: We also need rollback/canary strategies for model rollouts. If the POC is successful we may deploy to prod behind feature flags.

[07:43] Ravi Patel: Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automated fallback. You can pin routes to model versions and gradually shift traffic with metric-based gates. We'll include a rollout example in the docs.

[08:00] Elena Torres: One more — data residency. Our customers in EU require EU-only processing. Can the POC be restricted to eu-west-1?

[08:08] Maya Chen: Yes, we can run the POC in a specific region. For Dedicated/Private we can provision in eu-west-1 and ensure data doesn't exit the region. We'll note that in the infra checklist.

[08:20] Sana Ahmed: On telemetry — we need to be able to ingest traces into our Datadog. Is that supported?

[08:26] Ravi Patel: We can stream metrics and traces to your monitoring via OTLP/Datadog integration. We'll include example dashboards as part of the POC handover.

[08:40] Tom Becker: OK — good. Can you summarize the failure modes we should expect during spikes?

[08:48] Ravi Patel: Sure: 1) Cold-start latency when scaling new shards or replicas — mitigated by warm pools. 2) KV cache cold misses causing increased per-request compute — mitigated by warm caches and intelligent prefix caching. 3) Network congestion between shards — mitigated by colocating shards or choosing hosts with better interconnect. 4) Quality regressions from aggressive quantization — mitigated by per-prompt validation. 5) Cost overruns if burst is frequent — mitigated by burst budget and automated throttles.

[09:20] Elena Torres: That gives confidence. Let's lock dates. Can you run the benchmark next week, Wednesday 2026-04-21?

[09:28] Maya Chen: Tentatively yes — pending your traces and staging access. We'll block time for SE-led run and invite your infra folks.

[09:35] Mark Li: We'll send the traces today. Expect an S3 link.

[09:40] Maya Chen: Great. Action recap: Maya to send POC pricing/security docs; Ravi to deliver test plan; Mark to send traces; Sana to confirm VPC needs. We'll meet after the bench to review results. Any final questions?

[09:55] Elena Torres: None from me — thanks.

[10:00] Maya Chen: Thanks all — talk soon.

End of call.
